name: Licochalcone A

lead: Licochalcone A is a compound from licorice root used in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin, giving calmer, clearer skin. It is also discussed for possible brightening through reduced pigment production.

Laboratory work reports antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activity, and licorice flavonoids have been tested for tyrosinase inhibition. Human data come from acne trials of moisturizers that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so its own contribution cannot be separated.

paras: It is used in leave-on moisturizers and serums for redness-prone or breakout-prone skin, usually as one of several actives in a daily routine.
The sources reviewed give no skin safety data. Wikipedia lists generic hazard labeling for the pure chemical, which relates to handling rather than finished products.

angle.text: Used in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin to soothe irritation and leave skin calmer and clearer, and discussed for brightening via less pigment. Human data are acne trials of multi-ingredient moisturizers.

lead: Licochalcone A is a chalcone-type phenol isolated from the roots of licorice species (Glycyrrhiza inflata and G. glabra) [1][2]. In skincare it appears in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin and is also discussed for its possible effect on pigment production [3].

Laboratory research has reported antioxidant, antibacterial, antimalarial and anticancer activity [1][4][5][6], and licorice flavonoids have been examined for tyrosinase inhibition [3]. Human data on appearance come from acne trials of moisturizers that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so the contribution of licochalcone A alone cannot be separated [7][8].

paras: Six licorice flavonoids including licochalcone A were characterised in a 2013 study for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity [2]. A 1998 study reported superoxide-scavenging and antioxidative activity of retrochalcones from G. inflata [9]. A 2005 study isolated licorice flavonoids and tested their inhibitory effect on tyrosinase [3]. Other lab work reported activity against Plasmodium falciparum, bacteria and Helicobacter pylori, and against prostate cancer cells [4][5][6][10].

A completed phase 3 trial (n=120) tested a moisturizer containing licochalcone A, L-carnitine and 1,2-decanediol alongside adapalene gel in acne [7]. A completed trial (n=50) tested a moisturizer containing licochalcone A, decanediol, L-carnitine and salicylic acid for reducing acne relapse [8]. Both used multi-ingredient products, and results are not in the sources reviewed. No studies found on licochalcone A alone for pigmentation or redness.

timeline.event: Licochalcone A reported as an antimalarial agent in vitro [4].
Licorice flavonoids examined for tyrosinase inhibition [3].
